canonical_topic: Forward power market vs. daily (spot) power auctions
definition: The forward power market and the daily spot auction are related but structurally distinct markets: the spot auction sets the reference prices the forward market trades against, but access, contract types, and lot sizes differ sharply.
core_idea: Daily power auctions are restricted to entities that can physically generate and deliver power onto the grid, and trade in arbitrarily small sizes for immediate delivery anywhere; the forward market is open to any sufficiently capitalized participant, trades both physical and cash-settled financial contracts, but only in large monthly blocks at a limited set of hub locations.
key_points: Daily auctions (a.k.a. spot power market) are open only to power providers with generation/delivery capability.
Forward market participation requires no generation capability at all.
Forward contracts can be physical (delivery required) or financial (cash-settled).
Spot power can be bought in small sizes anywhere; forward power trades only in monthly blocks at roughly 30 major locations.
Most speculative trading activity occurs in the forward market.
relationships: Forward market prices are anchored to daily auction (spot) prices even though the two markets have different access rules and contract structures.
trading_implications: Speculators without generation assets can only participate via the forward market, not the daily auctions.
Because forward contracts are large and location-limited, achieving an exact regional price often requires a combination of a hub trade plus a separate fine-tuning trade.
caveats: The forward and spot markets are not the same market at different tenors — they have fundamentally different access requirements and contract sizes.
